poster.title: The Hobbit
poster.bookOrigin: English-language novel by J.R.R. Tolkien, published in London in 1937.
poster.creator: J.R.R. Tolkien
poster.alt: A photographed Hobbit jacket with pale pointed mountains, blue skies, green foreground woods, patterned borders and large cream lettering; a strip of spine remains visible.
poster.blurb: Pointed peaks and smaller tree crowns repeat a rhythm at different scales.

notes.title: The displayed edition
notes.body: George Allen & Unwin, London, 1937; photographed first-issue printed jacket. This is the blue, black and green printed object, not the differently coloured original artwork.

notes.title: Writing and image-making
notes.body: Tolkien wrote the novel and made its visual designs. The Tolkien Estate documents his art; the linked object record identifies the photographed printed jacket.

notes.title: A visible design relationship
notes.body: The cream title shares its colour with the mountain peaks. Complete foreground trees and their roots form a nearer band beneath the mountains.

studyData.intro: This photographed 1937 printed jacket brings mountains, woods, runes and title into one patterned landscape. Its visible spine and physical wear are retained; the study does not substitute Tolkien’s differently coloured original artwork.

regions.label: Pale letters among pale peaks
regions.summary: The large Hobbit lettering crosses blue and dark mountain faces.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: The large Hobbit lettering crosses blue and dark mountain faces. Its pale strokes echo the light tips of the peaks surrounding it.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The title becomes part of the landscape’s colour structure. It can remain readable because its regular letter shapes differ from the jagged ridges.

sections.heading: A compact name
sections.body: The English title is split between the small The and the much larger Hobbit. Their different sizes are part of the visible hierarchy; the rune border is not transcribed from this angled photograph.

regions.question: Which helps the title stand out more: colour, shape or size?

regions.label: Mountains repeat without matching
regions.summary: A sequence of pointed peaks rises and falls across the jacket.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A sequence of pointed peaks rises and falls across the jacket. Pale faces alternate with dark and blue slopes.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The repeated points make a continuous range, while unequal heights create destinations for the eye. The largest peaks need not be read as a literal mapped route.

regions.question: How does the tallest peak change the balance of the whole range?

regions.label: Small marks in a wide sky
regions.summary: Tiny dark wing-like marks cross the pale sky above the peaks.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Tiny dark wing-like marks cross the pale sky above the peaks. They are much smaller and more widely separated than the mountain shapes.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: These small forms give the sky a second scale of activity. Their spacing can make the broad pale field feel more expansive.

regions.question: Would the sky seem equally large without these small marks?

regions.label: A circle interrupts the angles
regions.summary: A thin circular outline appears behind the mountain tips.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A thin circular outline appears behind the mountain tips. Part of the circle is concealed by the overlapping landscape.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The circle introduces a simple curved form among pointed ridges. Its partial concealment helps distinguish a farther sky from nearer mountains.

regions.question: What does the hidden part of the circle contribute to a sense of depth?

regions.label: Horizontal movement above the peaks
regions.summary: Uneven blue horizontal strokes extend into the pale upper sky.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Uneven blue horizontal strokes extend into the pale upper sky. They become shorter and more dispersed towards the open area.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The horizontal marks counter the upward movement of the peaks. Their changing lengths create a transition between a dense printed edge and open sky.

regions.question: Where does the striped sky begin to feel like open space?

regions.label: A complete foreground woodland
regions.summary: Green tree crowns sit above pale outlined trunks, dark gaps and exposed roots.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Green tree crowns sit above pale outlined trunks, dark gaps and exposed roots. The foreground continues into bands of ground beneath them.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: Keeping crowns and roots together makes a nearer woodland distinct from the mountains. Repeated small pointed crowns echo the peaks at another scale.

regions.question: How does the tree scale change your sense of the mountains’ distance?

regions.label: The writer signs a drawn landscape

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: J.R.R. Tolkien appears within the foreground woods, with a separate small by higher in the landscape. The name’s pale edges separate dark letter bodies from surrounding forms.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The author credit belongs to the picture rather than sitting in a detached white band. It asks the eye to discover a name within an already patterned setting.

sections.heading: One person writes and draws
sections.body: The Tolkien Estate documents Tolkien’s visual art as well as his writing. His work on illustrations, patterns and lettering helps place this jacket within a wider practice of imagining the world of the book in both words and images.

regions.question: Does placing the author inside the woods change how you relate words to image?

regions.label: A repeated angular frame
regions.summary: A narrow green and dark patterned border runs along the upper front panel, with matching treatment below.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A narrow green and dark patterned border runs along the upper front panel, with matching treatment below. Small angular marks repeat within it.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The border presents the landscape as a designed book surface. Its regularity also makes the more varied peaks and tree crowns feel less mechanical.

regions.question: How would the image feel if the patterned frame were removed?

regions.label: Curved bands lead between peaks
regions.summary: Several pale and green curved bands run through the lower mountain area.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Several pale and green curved bands run through the lower mountain area. They overlap darker slopes and lead towards the foreground trees.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The curves offer a gentler directional route through the angular terrain. They can suggest passage or distance without requiring an exact identification of every form.

regions.question: Which curve most clearly leads your eye from mountains to woodland?

regions.label: The photographed book remains visible
regions.summary: A narrow angled spine remains at the left of the crop.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A narrow angled spine remains at the left of the crop. Its lettering and patterns repeat parts of the front design at a different perspective.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The spine reminds us that this is a photograph of a printed object with depth. Flattening or repainting it would remove evidence of the particular copy being studied.

sections.heading: A printed 1937 jacket
sections.body: The object record identifies a 1937 George Allen & Unwin first edition in an unrestored first-issue jacket printed in blue, black and green. That printed object is the source here; an original design drawing would be a different object with different colour evidence.

regions.question: What do you learn from seeing the spine beside the front panel?

connections.label: Rhythms of points
connections.title: Peaks meet crowns
connections.text: Pointed ridges and the smaller pointed tree crowns repeat an angular rhythm at different distances.

connections.label: Landscape lettering
connections.title: A title among peaks
connections.text: Cream title strokes share their colour with the pale mountain tops.
